name: Tivoli Gardens
label: Tivoli Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Vesterbrogade' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Vesterbrogade' (way/495927322): point nearest the subject (419 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/314752241: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tivoli Gardens' (545 m across).

text.description: Tivoli Gardens is an amusement park and pleasure garden right in the middle of Copenhagen. It opened on 15 August 1843, which makes it the second-oldest operating amusement park in the world. From the start it mixed flower gardens, cafés and rides with buildings in the style of an imaginary Orient, and coloured lamps lit the grounds after dark. That mix is why it photographs so well. The Moorish-style Nimb building and the park gate make a bold, symmetrical front, and in the evening the lit arches and lanterns give you a ready-made subject. The wooden roller coaster Rutschebanen dates from 1914 and is still running. The Chinese-style pantomime theatre has stood here since 1874. The park is also the most visited in Scandinavia, with 4.25 million visitors in 2024, so expect people in your shots at busy times. For the classic front view, stand on the pavement on Vesterbrogade outside the main entrance, in front of the Nimb building. Stand square-on to the Nimb facade and fit in the gate and the lit arches. If you have time for a second angle, Rådhuspladsen gives a wider view from the city side. Tivoli Lake shows the Chinese Pagoda and Tivoli Castle reflected in the water at dusk, but that spot is inside the park, so you need an entry ticket.
text.geographic_location: Tivoli Gardens is in central Copenhagen, next to the Central rail station. The main entrance and the Nimb building face Vesterbrogade.
text.directions_text: Start from the Central rail station area in downtown Copenhagen, because the park sits right beside it. Head to the main entrance on Vesterbrogade, on the park's street side. This entrance is the viewpoint for the classic front shot. Rådhuspladsen, the second viewpoint, is on the city side of the park. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the pavement, so the facade and gate keep a natural shape. If the pavement is crowded and you cannot step back, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole front in. Keep the phone level so the edges do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Vesterbrogade (on the pavement outside the main entrance, in front of the Nimb building). The Moorish-style Nimb facade and the park gate, framed straight on, with the lit arches and lanterns as the focus after dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the centre of the gate with the middle of the frame, with the facade filling the upper part. Wait for a gap in the passers-by, or let a few people stay in the lower corner to show scale. For a different view, try Rådhuspladsen for the park's skyline and lights in the distance with the square in front. Tivoli Lake, inside the park, is the choice for reflections of the Pagoda and Tivoli Castle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, let night mode do its work and brace your elbows against your body or a railing. Tap on the brightest lit arches to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights keep their colour and detail instead of burning out. Take a few frames and keep the sharpest one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the facade is lit. If you would rather have fewer people in the frame, an early-morning visit is quieter, but the lights will not be the main feature then.

text.access_note: The pavement on Vesterbrogade outside the entrance is public, but the park itself (including the lake view) needs an entry ticket, so check the official site before you go for dates and opening times.
claims_not_in_sources: The Vesterbrogade pavement and Rådhuspladsen are outside the park and free to stand in.
The lake view of the Chinese Pagoda and Tivoli Castle is inside the ticketed park, so you need an entry ticket.
The park is busiest in the evening, and early morning is quieter.
The Nimb facade is lit after dark and is the most photographed facade in the park (from a single guide, so worth checking on site).
Rådhuspladsen is on the city side of the park and gives a wider view of the park's skyline and lights.
The lake's name on the map may differ from 'Tivoli Lake' and should be checked on site.

name: Nyhavn
label: Nyhavn
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nyhavnsbroen' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Nyhavnsbroen' (way/4375853): middle (29 m across).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (2026-11-21T22:55).

text.description: Nyhavn is the old canal harbour in the middle of Copenhagen, lined with tall, brightly painted townhouses and moored wooden ships. It was dug between 1670 and 1675 under King Christian V and was once a busy, rowdy port. Today the quay is pedestrianised and the old ships are part of a heritage harbour. It photographs well because the colours, the water and the masts all sit in one straight line, so even a quick snap looks composed. The north side has the oldest house, No. 9, dating from 1681. Hans Christian Andersen lived at several addresses here, including No. 67. The classic picture is taken from the bridge over the canal, where the full row of houses, boats and water fits in one frame. If the bridge is too crowded, Inderhavnsbroen, the footbridge and cycle bridge across the harbour mouth, gives a view of Nyhavn from the water side. Expect people on the quayside and café terraces, so leave a little space around your subject and take a few shots as the crowd shifts. Keep the phone steady against the railing, and wipe the lens first, as harbour air can leave a faint film on it.
text.geographic_location: Nyhavn is in central Copenhagen, running from the square Kongens Nytorv down to the Inner Harbour, just south of the Royal Playhouse.
text.directions_text: Start at Kongens Nytorv, the square at the inner end of Nyhavn. The Kongens Nytorv Metro station is at the far side of the square and is served by all four Copenhagen Metro lines. If you arrive by harbour bus, the stop is next to the Royal Playhouse at the mouth of Nyhavn. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for natural-looking houses. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the bridge is busy and you cannot step back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as a single boat, a mast or a row of window frames.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Nyhavnsbroen (bridge at the canal's inner end; sources disagree on which end, so check on the map). The full row of coloured canal houses with moored wooden boats and the water in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the quay up with one of the lower grid lines so the houses stay upright. Put the boats in the lower third and the houses in the middle, with a little sky above. For a different view, walk to Inderhavnsbroen for Nyhavn seen across the water; it opens for boats, so stand clear of the central section when the horn sounds.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the houses to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and the bright colours do not wash out. Take a Live Photo too, as boats and passers-by can give you a better frame than the still you aimed for.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: One guide recommends late afternoon. The north-side houses are said to catch good light mainly in the morning and early afternoon in summer, and the terraces fill up from late morning, so going early means fewer people.

text.access_note: The quay is an open, pedestrianised public space and the museum ships can be seen from the cobbles; check the official site before you go if you want to board a ship or visit a museum.

text.description:
Rosenborg Castle is a Dutch Renaissance building in Copenhagen, set in the King's Garden (Kongens Have). It began as a country summerhouse in 1606, was extended several times and reached its present form by 1624. Christian IV was behind it, and it is one of his many building projects. Danish rulers lived here until around 1710, and it was used as a royal residence only twice after that, both times in emergencies. Today it is a museum of the Royal Collections and holds the Crown Jewels. It has been open to the public since 1838.

It photographs well because the castle stands in open parkland. In summer, flowers bloom in the castle garden, which can add colour in the foreground. The garden is the country's oldest royal garden and is busy with visitors, so wait a moment for a clear gap in the people on the paths.

Start with a wide shot of the full castle, then move in with zoom for the towers, rooflines and brickwork. Keep your phone level so the tall walls do not lean. Interior photography, if allowed at all, is a separate matter, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Rosenborg Castle stands inside Kongens Have (the King's Garden) in Copenhagen. Next to it are the barracks of the Royal Life Guards.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. From there the castle lies about 85 metres to the south-east, roughly 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 65 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole castle and its garden. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for towers, roof details and windows. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk much closer and want the full height in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 65 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. This gives you the castle with open garden in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the castle on one of the vertical lines, with the building in the upper two-thirds and paths or flowerbeds below. Keep the phone upright and level so the walls stay straight. Wait for a gap in the walkers if you want an empty foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the castle walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the brick and roof detail do not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. In summer the flowers in the garden add colour.

text.access_note: The castle is open to the public for tours as a museum and the garden is a public park, but access and tickets can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Amalienborg
label: Amalienborg
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/378106484: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Amalienborg' (383 m across).

text.description:
Amalienborg is the home of the Danish monarch and royal family, and it makes a tidy, satisfying photo because everything is arranged around one space. Four matching Classical palaces face each other across an octagonal square, with a large equestrian statue of Frederick V in the middle. That symmetry gives you strong lines and an easy composition, even if you only have a minute.

The palaces were built from 1750 and finished in 1760, as town mansions for four noble families. The royal family bought them after the Christiansborg Palace fire of 1794 and moved in, and today King Frederik X and Queen Mary live here. The outsides are identical, which is why the square feels so balanced, while the interiors are in the Rococo style.

For a phone, the aim is to show the whole square and then pick out details. Start wide so the palace fronts, the statue and the open space all fit. Then step closer or zoom for the statue against the façades, or for the stonework and windows. Keep the gridlines on and line up the statue with the gap between two palaces. If the statue looks too small, move a few steps towards it rather than cropping afterwards. Take a few frames with and without people in them, as the square can be busy.
text.geographic_location: Amalienborg is in Frederiksstaden, the district just outside the old walled city of Indre By in central Copenhagen. The four palaces surround one octagonal square.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Indre By, the old city centre, and walk to Amalienborg Slotsplads, the palace square. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m north-east of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the square and several palace fronts. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the statue with a palace behind it. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for façade details and the top of the statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m north-east of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. The palaces and the statue should be close by, so look for the matching palace fronts and the statue from here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the gridlines on and keep the statue on a vertical line, with the palace fronts level along a horizontal line. Hold the phone steady and level, because the straight edges of the buildings will show any tilt. For a second picture, move in close and use the statue as a foreground shape with the palaces behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the palace façade to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Live Photos can be fun if people or flags are moving, but hold still for a second afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the square. Midday sun can be harsh on the pale façades.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the palaces are a royal residence and only some parts are open to visitors, so check the official site before you go.

name: Christiansborg Palace
label: Christiansborg
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Marmorbroen' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Marmorbroen' (way/379074390): middle (44 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25992657: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Christiansborg Palace' (398 m across).

text.description: Christiansborg Palace sits on the islet of Slotsholmen in the middle of Copenhagen, and it is the one building where Denmark's Parliament, the Prime Minister's Office and the Supreme Court all work under one roof. It is also the third palace on this site. The first castle here was built in 1167, and the current Neo-baroque building was put up between 1907 and 1928 after two earlier palaces were lost to fires, in 1794 and 1884. Its granite-faced walls, copper roof and tall central tower make a big, solid subject, and it is large enough that you will want to stand back to fit it in. Guides call the stone bridge Marmorbroen the classic angle for a phone shot. From there the palace gate, the castle square and the main building line up in a neat, centred composition, with the bridge's balustrades and lanterns in the foreground and the canal below. The tower is 106 metres tall and is the tallest in the city, so it works well as the high point of a vertical shot. Parts of the palace are open to the public, including the ruins of the older castles beneath it, but the outside view from the bridge needs no ticket. Take a wide shot first, then move in on details such as the lanterns or the gate.
text.geographic_location: Christiansborg Palace is on the islet of Slotsholmen in central Copenhagen, surrounded by canals.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is given for this spot, so head for Slotsholmen in central Copenhagen. Follow the map from there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the symmetrical view of the gate and main building. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the palace will not fit, or to the telephoto (2x or more) to pick out the tower and the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Marmorbroen. A symmetrical, centred view of the palace gate, the castle square and the main building, framed by the stone balustrades and lanterns of the bridge. The exact best spot can vary, so check on the day and adjust your position a little to find the cleanest view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the palace gate on the centre line, so the shot looks symmetrical. If you are on Marmorbroen, let the bridge's balustrades and lanterns fill the foreground, and include the canal if it is calm enough to show reflections. For a different angle, Højbro Plads shows the palace tower above the canal with the Marble Bridge in the middle distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the palace walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its colour and the building does not turn too dark. Keep the phone level so the tower stays upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or golden hour, when the light is softest on the water.

text.access_note: The view from the bridge is from a public place, but only some parts of the palace are open to visitors, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

label: Christiania
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Prinsessegade' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Prinsessegade' (way/776583734): point nearest the subject (150 m long).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/250989045: large area 'Freetown Christiania' (1827 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Freetown Christiania is a self-governing community in the Christianshavn part of Copenhagen. It began in 1971, when people moved into a disused military base, and it now covers about 7.7 hectares with roughly 850 to 1,000 residents. The area takes in old barracks and part of the 17th-century ramparts that Christianshavn still keeps. The ramparts date from 1617 and are counted among the finest surviving defence works of their age. Four gunpowder storehouses from 1779–1780 also still stand there.

For a first photo, start at the main red steel gate on Prinsessegade. It is the community's symbolic entrance, and the painted entry area and the start of the lanes make a strong, colourful frame. Guides say photographing the gate itself is allowed. It gets busy later in the day, so an early visit gives a cleaner picture.

Photography rules here are mixed. Do not photograph Pusher Street or any signed no-photo zone, and ask residents before photographing them or their homes. If you want a calmer view afterwards, Christianshavns Vold shows the lake and canal with the self-built houses beyond the water. Dyssebroen has colourful waterfront houses and tree-lined paths. Keep your phone away from faces and front doors, and look for signs as you go.
text.geographic_location: Christiania sits in the Christianshavn district of Copenhagen, on the island of Amager. It occupies the former barracks and part of the old ramparts, with its main gate on Prinsessegade.
text.directions_text: No Metro, train or tram stop is listed close by; head for Prinsessegade and the red gate in the Christianshavn area. Follow the signs once you are inside. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the red gate and the entrance plaza. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the gate and painted entry area will not fit. Use telephoto (2x or more) for painted walls and details, not for people.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Prinsessegade (at the main red steel gate, the community's entrance). The gate and entrance plaza, with the painted entry area and the start of the community's lanes.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the gate in the centre or on one third line, keeping the painted entry area in the lower part of the frame. Wait a moment for people to pass so the gate stays clear. For a different view, Christianshavns Vold shows the canal and the community's houses across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright, so the red and the paint colours do not wash out. Do not point the phone at Pusher Street or at signed no-photo areas.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before about 09:30 gives a cleaner shot of the gate, according to one guide. It tends to be busy later in the day.

text.access_note: The community is open to visitors, but it has its own rules and signed no-photo zones, and photography rules vary, so check the official site and the signs before you go.

name: The Little Mermaid
label: Little Mermaid
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/25074274: the OpenStreetMap point 'The Little Mermaid'.

text.description:
The Little Mermaid (Den lille Havfrue) is a small bronze statue of a mermaid becoming human, sitting on a rock at the water's edge on the Langelinie promenade. It is only 1.25 metres tall, so many visitors are surprised by how modest it looks. That works in your favour: the statue, the rock and the water make a simple, uncluttered picture, with open harbour behind it.

The statue was commissioned in 1909 by Carl Jacobsen, the son of Carlsberg's founder, after he was captivated by a ballet of Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tale. Edvard Eriksen made it, and it was unveiled on 23 August 1913. Eriksen's wife, Eline, was the model for the figure.

For a good phone photo, think of it as a small subject with a lot of space around it. Use gridlines and place the mermaid on one of the thirds, leaving the water and sky as breathing room. The rock is close to the water and there is often a small crowd, so be patient and wait for a gap, or shoot between groups. Take a wide shot first to show the setting, then a closer one to show her face and pose. Keep your distance from the rock and do not climb on it. Tap on the statue to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the bronze stays detailed instead of turning into a silhouette.
text.geographic_location: The statue is on the Langelinie promenade, on the waterside in Copenhagen's harbour area. It sits on a rock just off the path at the water's edge.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Langelinie promenade in Copenhagen. Once you are on the promenade, follow the waterside path to the statue. The phone icon on the map is about 10 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue with its rock and water. Then try telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot without leaning over the rocks. The ultra-wide (0.5x) is useful only if you want a lot of harbour and sky, and it will make the statue look very small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 10 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the statue on one of the thirds, leaving space on the side she faces. Wait for a gap in the crowd, and keep the rock's edge and the water in the frame so the shot shows where she sits. For a tighter portrait-style shot, move to the telephoto lens rather than walking closer to the rock.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the bronze keeps its detail. Take a few frames in a row, as people tend to wander into the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day, when there are usually fewer people at the rock. Soft, even light, such as a bright overcast day, suits the dark bronze well.

text.access_note: The statue stands at the waterside on the Langelinie promenade, but check the official site before you go for any local restrictions or works.

name: Strøget
label: Strøget
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Amagertorv' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Amagertorv' (way/24721845): middle (212 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1629331: large area 'Strøget' (1089 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description: Strøget is Copenhagen's long car-free shopping street, running through the middle of the old city for about 1.1 km. It is really a chain of streets and small squares rather than one straight line, and the best-looking part for a phone photo is Amagertorv. Here the Stork Fountain (Storkespringvandet) sits in the open, and the pedestrian street runs away from you with shopfronts on both sides. The paving helps too: Amagertorv was resurfaced in 1993 in a granite pattern designed by the artist Bjørn Nørgaard, which gives you an interesting foreground. The street became pedestrian-only on 17 November 1962, at first as a trial, and the change was made permanent in 1964. Because it is closed to cars, you can stand in the street and take your time over the shot. It gets very busy, though. Around 80,000 people can use it on a summer day. If you want clear pavement and a calm scene, go early in the morning. If you want a second angle, Nytorv has the columned courthouse facade closing the view at the end of the street. The ILLUM rooftop gives a raised view down over Amagertorv, with Christiansborg Palace beyond the rooftops, but it is inside a department store, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Strøget runs through the centre of Copenhagen's old city, between City Hall Square (Rådhuspladsen) in the west and Kongens Nytorv in the east. Amagertorv, the square with the Stork Fountain, is one of the pedestrian squares along it.
text.directions_text: Amagertorv is one of the squares along Strøget, and the Stork Fountain stands on it. Kongens Nytorv, the large square at the eastern end of Strøget, has a Metro station, which is a useful place to arrive. From there, follow the pedestrian streets to the fountain and check a map on your phone. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which gives a natural view of the street. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the patterned paving and the shopfronts on both sides. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the fountain or people further down the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Amagertorv (stand by the Stork Fountain (Storkespringvandet) and face along the street). The fountain square with the pedestrian street running away from you, with patterned pavement and shopfronts framing the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and keep the street centred, with the vertical lines of the buildings straight. Crouch a little so more of the granite pattern fills the lower part of the picture. For a different view, Nytorv shows the columned courthouse facade at the end of the street, and the ILLUM rooftop looks down over Amagertorv.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the fountain or a shopfront to set focus, then use the exposure slider to stop bright sky or shop windows washing out. Take a few frames, as people keep walking through the scene. Live Photos can help you pick a moment with fewer people in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds build up, when the paving is nearly empty. Midday is very crowded.

text.access_note: Strøget and Amagertorv are open, car-free public space; the ILLUM rooftop is inside a department store, so check the official site before you go.

name: The Black Diamond (Royal Library)
label: Black Diamond
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cirkelbroen' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cirkelbroen' (way/419513906): middle (43 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/19856927: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Den Sorte Diamant' (193 m across).

text.description:
The Black Diamond is the waterfront extension to the Royal Danish Library on Slotsholmen, in central Copenhagen. It is named for its polished black granite and its tilting, irregular shape. Schmidt Hammer Lassen designed it, and it was completed in 1999, opening to the public on 15 September that year. The box leans towards the water, and a wide glazed 'crevasse' splits the facade in two.

It photographs well because the dark stone works like a mirror. The granite is a type called Absolute Black, mined in Zimbabwe and cut and polished in Italy, and it covers about 2,500 square metres. On a calm day the canal and sky can show in the stone, and the sloping lines make a bold shape even from a distance.

One framing worth trying is from Cirkelbroen (the Circle Bridge), which sits opposite the Black Diamond across the canal. From there the building sits across the water, with the bridge's railings and curves in the foreground. Aim at the harbour-side facade, using the bridge to add depth to the picture.

For a second angle, walk along Christians Brygge, the road beside the building, and shoot the granite and the water in front of it with the ultra-wide lens. If you go inside, the atrium has views of the harbour through the big glass front. People are studying there, so keep your phone quiet and don't use flash.
text.geographic_location: On Slotsholmen in central Copenhagen, on the harbour side of the Royal Library. Christians Brygge, a busy road, separates it from the library's older Holm Building.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so I can't give a public-transport route. From there the Black Diamond is to the north. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tilted facade and the bridge railings in the frame. If the building looks too small or the edges look stretched, switch to the default lens (1x). Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of the granite and the glass crevasse.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Cirkelbroen (across Christianshavns Kanal, facing the Black Diamond's harbour-side facade). The black granite facade of the Black Diamond across the canal, with the Circle Bridge in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals straight so the leaning building looks deliberate. Place part of the bridge railing or curve low in the frame as a foreground. Leave some water in the picture to catch the reflection. For an alternative, walk along Christians Brygge and shoot the facade and the water in front of it with the ultra-wide lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the black stone keeps its detail. Take a few shots at slightly different exposures. A Live Photo can catch passing boats or ripples on the canal. Indoors, leave the flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. A calm, still day gives the clearest reflections in the canal and the granite.

text.access_note: The outside views are from public space, but the library's opening hours and any rules for the interior can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: The Round Tower
label: Round Tower
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1011492033: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Round Tower' (22 m across).

text.description: The Round Tower (Rundetårn) is a 17th-century brick tower in the old centre of Copenhagen, built for King Christian IV as an astronomical observatory. It photographs well because it is so simple: a plain cylinder wrapped in bands of yellow and red brick, which are the Oldenburg family colours. The pattern gives your picture strong lines and clear colour even on a grey day. The foundation stone was laid in 1637 and the tower was finished in 1642. It is 34.8 metres to the platform at the top. Inside, a gently sloping spiral corridor of about 7.5 turns takes you up, rather than steps. The tower is joined at the back to Trinitatis Church and has never been a church tower itself. A famous story says Peter the Great rode up it on horseback in 1716. For a phone photo, the practical position is anywhere on the public ground next to the tower's base. You may need to step back from the tower, or use the ultra-wide lens, to fit the whole tower in the frame. Once you have one clean shot of the whole tower, move in for a close-up of the brick stripes. Keep your phone upright and level to stop the tower leaning backwards in the frame. If you go up, the platform has views over the city, but check the official site before you go for access details.
text.geographic_location: The Round Tower stands in the old centre of Copenhagen, attached to Trinitatis Church and close to the University of Copenhagen and the Regensen dormitories.
text.directions_text: Navigate to Rundetårn (the Round Tower) using your phone's maps app. You are in the right place as soon as you reach the base of the tower. Look for the tall brick cylinder with yellow and red bands. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the tower as you see it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough to fit the whole height in. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the brick bands and the details on the upper part of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on the public ground right beside the base and face the wall. Step back along the building line if you want more of the tower in the frame. Stay close to the base for dramatic upward shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the tower with the vertical lines. Hold the phone as upright as you can, because tilting it upwards makes the tower lean back. Place the top of the tower near the upper third of the frame, with a little sky above. For a second picture, zoom in until the yellow and red stripes fill the frame and the curve of the wall runs diagonally.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the brick to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not turn white and the colours stay rich. If you use ultra-wide, keep the tower in the middle of the frame to limit stretching at the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even daylight shows the brick colours best, and early in the day is often quieter around the base.

text.access_note: The outside of the tower can be photographed from the surrounding public space, but climbing it may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Frederik's Church (the Marble Church)
label: Marble Church
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25524833: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Marble Church' (74 m across).

text.description: Frederik's Church, known to most people as the Marble Church, is the focal point of the Frederiksstaden district and sits due west of Amalienborg Palace. Its big green-grey dome, with gold window frames and statues along the outer walls, makes it easy to spot and rewarding to photograph. The dome has a span of 31 metres, the largest of any church dome in Scandinavia, and it rests on twelve columns. The church was planned by Nicolai Eigtved around 1740, and the foundation stone was laid in 1749. Work then stalled for a very long time, and the building stood unfinished for nearly 150 years. It was completed to a design by Ferdinand Meldahl and opened on 19 August 1894. Despite the nickname, it was built mainly of limestone rather than marble, because of money worries. For a phone photo, the appeal is the mix of a rounded dome, a columned front portico and the statues of church figures around the grounds, which gives you both a wide view and plenty of close details. Gold lettering runs across the front portico, and a statue of Grundtvig stands at the entrance. Stand back far enough to fit the dome and front together, then step closer for the statues and lettering. Keep the phone level so the columns stay straight, and keep passers-by out of the lower edge of the frame if you can.
text.geographic_location: In the Frederiksstaden district of central Copenhagen, the church stands due west of Amalienborg Palace and is the focal point of the surrounding streets.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so go by taxi or hired scooter to the Frederiksstaden area next to Amalienborg Palace, then look west for the dome. The phone icon on the map is about 55 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the dome and front of the church in one frame. Switch to the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome, gold details and statues. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move close and want the columns and portico in one shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 55 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west. This distance lets the 1x lens take in the whole building without tilting the phone steeply upwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the church up with the central grid lines so the dome sits in the middle and the walls look straight. Include a little foreground, such as paving or a tree, to give a sense of scale. Then zoom in for a second shot of the dome and statues. Take an extra close-up of the gold lettering on the portico if you can get near it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dome to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out the stonework. Take a few frames, as people often walk through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Under a bright midday sky the dome can look flat, so use the exposure slider to keep some detail.

text.access_note: The church is a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any dress or behaviour expectations inside; the outside and grounds are what you see from the stand-here point.

name: Børsen (the old Stock Exchange)
label: Børsen
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Børsbroen' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Børsbroen' (way/379074386): middle (46 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3860938969: the OpenStreetMap point 'The Danish Chamber of Commerce'.
notes: Damaged by fire in 2024; restoration under way.

text.description: Børsen is the old Stock Exchange, a long red-brick building on the island of Slotsholmen, right next to Christiansborg Palace. Christian IV had it built in the early 1600s, and it is a leading example of the Dutch Renaissance style in Denmark. It is about 128 m long, so the facade is a long run of red-brick gables. That is why it works as a photograph from across the water. The building is best known for its dragon spire, made of four twisted dragon tails. The spire fell in the fire of 16 April 2024, and the building is now being rebuilt. The plan uses traditional materials, including more than 800,000 handmade red bricks, with completion projected for 2029. For now, the facade and gables are the subject, not the spire, and you cannot see the interior. From the canal side you can take in the brick facade and its gables with the palace nearby. If you have time, there are two other options. Slotsholmsgade gives a contrast shot of the building against the Christiansborg tower. Knippelsbro gives a view down Børsgade toward Børsen, with street traffic in the foreground. A free visitor centre with views over the site opened in February 2026, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Børsen stands on Slotsholmen in the centre of Copenhagen, beside Christiansborg Palace. It sits on the north side of the embankment that leads toward Christianshavn.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so walk to Slotsholmen, next to Christiansborg Palace. Head for the canal side of Børsen, at or near the viewpoint that guides call Børsbroen. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the facade and gables in one frame. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want more sky and water. Try 2x or 3x on a telephoto phone to pick out one gable or the brickwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Børsbroen (canal side, looking toward Christiansborg). The red-brick Dutch Renaissance facade and its gables along the canal, with the palace nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the facade up with a horizontal line so the long building sits level. Keep a strip of canal in the foreground. Because the spire is gone, make the gables and brickwork the main subject. For a different angle, try Slotsholmsgade for Børsen against the Christiansborg tower, or Knippelsbro for the view down Børsgade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to focus. Then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Hold the phone upright and keep it level so the vertical lines do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or evening light works best for facade photos from the canal side.

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from outside in public space, but the building is under reconstruction and a visitor centre has opened, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Building-site screens or scaffolding may partly cover the facade, so the view can change from visit to visit.
Holding the phone level and using gridlines helps keep vertical lines from leaning in a wide shot of a long building.
Lowering the exposure slider helps stop a bright sky washing out when the facade is in shade.

name: Copenhagen Opera House
label: Opera House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Amalienborg Slotsplads' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Amalienborg Slotsplads' (way/1307538577): middle (262 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1088494374: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Copenhagen Opera House' (228 m across).
notes: Seen across the harbour from Amalienborg.

text.description: Copenhagen Opera House, usually called Operaen, is Denmark's national opera house. It sits on the island of Holmen, right on the Inner Harbour, and it photographs well because of how it is lined up. The architect Henning Larsen placed it in alignment with Amalienborg and the Marble Church, so the view across the water is unusually tidy and balanced. A big glass front and a wide, flat roof give the building strong horizontal lines, and the water in front doubles them when the harbour is calm. The building opened on 15 January 2005 and has 14 floors, five of them below ground, so most of its size is out of sight. Guides often call this the most symmetrical view of the building. For your phone, keep the horizon level and let the fountain and the water frame the shot. If you would like a second angle, Inderhavnsbroen gives an open view across the inner harbour with the bridge in the frame. The Opera is a working theatre with guided tours inside, so for anything beyond the outside view, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Opera House is on the island of Holmen in central Copenhagen, on the shore of the Inner Harbour and directly across the water from the royal palace of Amalienborg.
text.directions_text: Head for Amalienborg Slotsplads, the square in front of the Amalienborg palace. The spot data lists no station or tram stop for this spot. Walk towards the water by the Amalie Garden fountain and you will see it straight ahead. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole building, the water and the fountain. Try the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the glass front and roofline. The ultra-wide (0.5x) is only worth it if you want a lot of foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Amalienborg Slotsplads (Amalienborg side, across the harbour from the Opera House). The Opera House seen straight on across the water, with the fountain in Amalie Garden in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the Opera's roofline along one of the horizontal lines. Centre the building so the scene stays symmetrical, and place the fountain low in the frame as foreground. Check that the horizon isn't tilted. If you have time, Inderhavnsbroen is a second spot, with the bridge in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the glass front to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out. Zoom in on the fountain spray and hold still. A Live Photo can catch moving water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or evening is likely to suit this view, because the sun will be behind you and falling on the front of the building. Calm, still days give the best reflections in the water.

text.access_note: Amalienborg Slotsplads is a public square, but the Opera House itself is a working theatre with guided tours and performances, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Amalienborg is in the Frederiksstaden district of Copenhagen.
From Amalienborg the viewer looks roughly south-east, so afternoon and evening sun is behind the viewer and lights the Opera's front, while morning sun may be towards the camera.
Calm water gives better reflections of the building.
The walk to the Opera round the harbour is longer than the straight line across the water.

name: Church of Our Saviour
label: Church of Our Saviour
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Wilders Plads' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Wilders Plads' (way/8128670): middle (9 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25607908: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Church of Our Saviour, Copenhagen' (69 m across).

text.description:
The Church of Our Saviour (Vor Frelsers Kirke) is a Dutch-baroque church in Christianshavn, and it is the spire that makes it so easy to photograph. The black and gold spire reaches 90 metres, and a staircase winds around the outside of it, turning four times anticlockwise. The walls are made of red and yellow tiles in a random pattern, and the roof is covered in black-glazed tiles. The church was designed by Lambert van Haven and inaugurated in 1695. The spire was designed by Lauritz de Thurah and finished in 1752. At the very top, a 4-metre figure of Christ stands on a gilded globe. It was made with exaggerated proportions because it was meant to be seen from far away.

For a phone photo, the best approach is to keep your distance. The houses give the picture scale and a sense of place, and the water adds a calm band underneath. If you want a closer look at the spire's structure, Prinsessegade also works, as the tower is seen up close from the street corner. Stay on the ground for these shots: the tower climb is a separate activity, so check the official site before you go if you plan to do it.
text.geographic_location: The church is in Christianshavn, the canal-lined district on the Amager side of Copenhagen's harbour, which Christian IV planned in 1617. The viewpoint on Wilders Plads is beside the Christianshavn Canal, north of the church.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Christianshavn itself and make your way to Wilders Plads, where you will find the canal. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the spire, the canal and the houses together. Switch to telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the spire. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only from Prinsessegade, where the tower is too close to fit in otherwise.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Wilders Plads. The church spire rising beyond the Christianshavn Canal, with the canal-side houses in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the spire on one of the vertical lines, with the houses along the bottom of the frame and the canal leading the eye towards it. Keep the phone level so the spire does not lean. If you want a closer view, Prinsessegade is a good alternative: the tower is seen up close from the street corner, close enough to show the spire's structure. Tilting the phone up there will make the tower lean, so step back as far as you can first.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the spire to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the gold detail and the sky stay clear rather than washed out. Take a few shots at 1x and 2x so you can compare them later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to the gold and the tiled walls than harsh midday sun, and a calm day gives a cleaner canal.

text.access_note: The viewpoint on Wilders Plads is open public space; the church interior and tower climb are separate, so check the official site before you go.

name: Botanical Garden palm house
label: Botanical Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Palmehuset' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Palmehuset' (way/264570191): middle (101 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/3098803: large area 'Botanical Garden' (669 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description: The Palm House is the centrepiece of the glasshouse complex in Copenhagen's Botanical Garden. It is a cast-iron and glass building that rises above a pond and lawn, so the water, the greenery and the glass make a tidy, layered picture. The complex dates from 1874 and was paid for by J. C. Jacobsen, the Carlsberg founder, who took his inspiration from the Crystal Palace in London. The Palm House itself is 16 metres tall, with narrow cast-iron spiral stairs up to a walkway at the top. The whole garden has been listed since 1977. The garden covers 10 hectares and is informal, so it is pleasant to wander round with your phone in hand. The best-known photo is taken from the lawn and pond in front of the glasshouse, looking up at the whole building with the water in the foreground. In autumn, fallen leaves around the pond add colour. Another option is inside: the walkway at the top gives a view down onto the palms with the glass dome overhead. That is a ticketed part of the visit, so check the official site before you go. Keep the whole building in the frame, use the pond to lead the eye upwards, and take a few shots at different distances so you have both a wide view and a close one of the ironwork.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Copenhagen, inside the University of Copenhagen Botanical Garden, whose address is Gothersgade 128. The Palm House stands at the heart of the garden's old glasshouse complex.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Botanical Garden at Gothersgade 128 in the centre of Copenhagen. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the whole Palm House and the pond fit in one frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the water and the building gets cropped. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the ironwork and the dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (from the lawn and pond in front of the glasshouse, looking up at it). The whole cast-iron and glass Palm House rising above the water in the foreground, with garden greenery around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the pond in the lower third, so the water leads the eye up to the glasshouse. Hold the phone level so the vertical iron frame stays straight. For a second picture, go up to the walkway inside, if you have bought a ticket, and shoot down onto the palms with the glass dome overhead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the glass to set focus and exposure, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and glass do not turn pale. Inside the warm hall, wipe your lens first, as it may mist up.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light, such as a bright overcast day, helps to keep reflections on the glass under control. Autumn adds fallen leaves around the pond.

text.access_note: The garden grounds are free to enter during opening hours, and the lawn and pond view is outdoors, but the Palm House itself charges admission, so check the official site before you go.

name: Gefion Fountain
label: Gefion Fountain
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).

text.description: The Gefion Fountain is a large fountain on the Copenhagen harbour front, in the Nordre Toldbod area next to Kastellet and just south of Langelinie. A group of oxen pulls a plough, driven by the Norse goddess Gefjon. It shows the old legend of how the island of Zealand, where Copenhagen stands, was ploughed out of the earth in a single night. It photographs well because it is full of movement: the animals strain forward, and spray rises around them when the water is running. The sculptor was Anders Bundgaard, who modelled the figures between 1897 and 1899. The basins and decoration were finished in 1908, and the fountain first ran on 14 July 1908. The Carlsberg Foundation gave it to the city to mark the brewery's 50th anniversary. After a long restoration it was re-inaugurated in September 2004. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for the full scene, then move in with the default lens (1x) or a zoom for the goddess and the straining oxen. Keep your phone level, or the fountain will look as if it is leaning. Wait a moment for people to move out of the foreground, or include one or two to show the scale.
text.geographic_location: The fountain is on the harbour front in the Nordre Toldbod area of Copenhagen, right beside Kastellet (the Citadel) and immediately south of Langelinie.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Kastellet and the Nordre Toldbod harbour front. The fountain stands right next to Kastellet, just south of Langelinie. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit the whole sculpture group and basin in. Then switch to the default lens (1x), or a 2x-5x zoom if your phone has one, for close shots of Gefjon and the oxen.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. You are close, so the group fills the frame and the ultra-wide lens is useful.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the figures on one of the vertical lines, with the oxen leading into the frame. Keep the horizon and basin edges level. For a tighter picture, zoom in on the goddess and the front pair of oxen, with the water behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sculpture to set focus and exposure, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky or the water is washing out. Try a Live Photo to catch the moving spray, and choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the water is running and the sunlight is not directly in your lens. From where you stand you are looking west, so morning light should fall on the front of the figures, while late-afternoon sun may come from in front of you and make them dark. Early in the day is also likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The fountain stands on the open harbour front, but check the official site before you go for any works, closures or times when the water is switched off.
claims_not_in_sources: From the stand-here point you look west towards the fountain, so morning sun should light the front of the figures and late-afternoon sun may come from in front of you.
Early in the day the harbour front is likely to be quieter than later on.
The water may be switched off at some times of year or for maintenance, so the spray may not always be visible.
The fountain is too large to fit fully in the frame at 1x from close to it.

name: Langelinie promenade

camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).

text.description: Langelinie is the long waterside promenade, pier and park north of Kastellet in central Copenhagen. The name means 'Long Line', and it goes back to the mid-17th century, when it described a path along the Øresund coast. For a long time the area was military ground, and later a toll kept ordinary people out of the park. It only opened to everybody after the public uprising of 1848. The harbour works finished in 1894 turned the old beach into harbour basins, and Langelinie became a pier on the far side of them. Today the park holds monuments, a marina and statues, and it is the home of The Little Mermaid. Most cruise ships arriving in Copenhagen berth at the pier. On the pier there is a bronze polar bear with cubs, which still shows bullet holes in its head from the Occupation. It photographs well because the path leads the eye along the water, with boats, ships and open sky around it. That gives you a clear foreground and background without much effort. Take a few wide frames of the whole stretch, then step closer for details such as the polar bear or the boats in the marina. If a cruise ship is in, it can fill the background, so it is worth checking which way you want to point before you shoot. Keep the horizon level using your phone's gridlines.
text.geographic_location: Langelinie is on the Øresund waterfront in central Copenhagen, just north of the fortress of Kastellet. The park runs north from Esplanaden to Langelinie Marina and the base of the pier.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed close to this spot, so start from central Copenhagen and make your way to the Langelinie area beside Kastellet. Head along the waterside path and let the map guide the last few metres. The phone icon on the map is about 200 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the length of the promenade, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as boats in the marina or a ship in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 200 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. From here you can follow the path towards it and use its line as your guide.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the path on a lower third line so it leads the eye into the picture. Keep the horizon over the water level. For a second picture, move in on one subject, such as the polar bear sculpture on the pier, and let the harbour blur behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Try a short Live Photo to catch walkers or boats moving past.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or the hour before sunset usually gives softer light and fewer walkers on the path.

text.access_note: This is a public waterside park and promenade, but check the official site before you go for any local restrictions or events.

name: Nyboder's yellow rows
label: Nyboder
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/8345807809: the OpenStreetMap point 'Nyboder'.

text.description:
Nyboder is a district of long, low terraced houses in Copenhagen, painted in a warm yellow that Danes use as a colour name in its own right. The area was begun in 1631 under Christian IV to house sailors of the Royal Danish Navy and their families. Most of what you see today was built from 1757, apart from a single row in Sankt Pauls Gade. The first houses were actually red and white, so the yellow is a later look. Naval, army and air force personnel still live here, so it is a real neighbourhood and not a museum.

It photographs well because of the repetition. Identical doors, windows and rooflines run away in straight lines, and the yellow walls stand out against the sky and the red brick of St Paul's Church, built in the 1870s in the middle of the area. The straight streets make it easy to line up a clean, symmetrical shot.

Take one wide view of a whole row, then a closer shot of a doorway or a run of windows. Keep your voice down and keep out of doorways and windows, as people live here.
text.geographic_location: Nyboder sits in central Copenhagen, just north of the old city centre. It lies close to Store Kongensgade and Øster Voldgade and not far south of Kastellet.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Nyboder area, near Store Kongensgade and Øster Voldgade, from the centre of Copenhagen, by taxi or hired scooter. The phone icon on the map is about 130 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a whole row. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) in the narrowest streets, and to the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to squeeze the rows together and pick out doors and windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 130 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Face that way for the first frame, then walk towards the rows and shoot along the street from the pavement edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the rooflines up with them so the rows look straight and the verticals do not lean. Stand in the middle of the street's line of view so the rows meet at a point in the distance. For a simple detail shot, fill the frame with one yellow wall and a single door. Do not point your phone into windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a yellow wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the yellow stays rich and does not wash out to pale cream. Avoid portrait mode on the buildings themselves, as it can blur the edges of the rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Low sun in the morning or late afternoon usually gives the warmest colour on the yellow walls. Early in the day the streets are likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The rows are streets with homes that are still lived in, so keep to the public streets and be considerate; check the official site before you go if you want to see anything beyond the streets themselves.

name: St. Alban's Church
label: St. Alban's Church
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/36790389: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Alban's Anglican Church' (39 m across).

text.description: St. Alban's Church, often called simply the English Church, is an Anglican church in a calm park setting at the end of Amaliegade, right beside the Kastellet citadel, the Gefion Fountain and Langelinie. It was built between 1885 and 1887 for the growing English congregation in Copenhagen, and was designed by Arthur Blomfield as a traditional English parish church in the Gothic Revival style. It photographs well because it looks so unlike most Copenhagen buildings. The walls use knapped flint, which is unusual in Denmark but common in the south of England, and the spire is made of Åland stone. The tower holds fifteen tubular bells, and the shutters in the tower open every quarter-hour while they chime, so the tower is worth a look even if you are only passing. Tall, pointed windows and steep roof lines give you strong shapes to work with. The simplest picture is the whole church with trees and lawn around it, which shows off the park setting. Then move closer or zoom in for the flint texture and the spire. Keep the phone level so the tower stays straight, and watch for people on the paths if you want a clean frame.
text.geographic_location: St. Alban's Church stands in the northern part of Copenhagen's city centre, at the end of Amaliegade. It sits on the park-like esplanade next to the Kastellet citadel, close to the Gefion Fountain and Langelinie.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from the Kastellet and Gefion Fountain area, which is right next to the church, or from the top of Amaliegade, and walk to St. Alban's Church, also known as the English Church. The phone icon on the map is about 35 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole church in its park. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the tower, spire and flint walls. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk right up to the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it stays straight. Keep some lawn and trees in the foreground to show the park setting. Then zoom in on the spire or the flint and stone texture for a second shot. Avoid tilting the phone upwards, as the tower will lean; step back instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the pale stone keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning is likely to suit this side of the church, as the sun should be behind you and light up the walls. A soft, overcast day also shows the flint texture well.

text.access_note: The church grounds sit in an open park area, but this is a working church, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: From the stand-here point, looking west, morning sun is likely to be behind the photographer and light the church walls facing east.
Overcast light tends to show the texture of flint and stone well.
The ground around the church is open and walkable for visitors.
Tilting a phone upwards makes tall towers appear to lean inwards.
A working church may have restricted or changing hours for visitors going inside.
